item.title: 3 Ways Meditation or Yoga Could Improve Mood, Extend Life
item.description:
Meditation

3 Ways Meditation or Yoga Could Improve Mood, Extend Life

Evolving research shows consistent mindfulness practice points toward longevity.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • Telomere length is a marker of aging well and decreased susceptibility to chronic illness.
  • Like little caps on the ends of chromosomes to keep them strong and vital, telomeres preserve health.
  • You needn’t be a Buddhist monk or practice yoga asanas all day to benefit from these “new” life extenders.
Source: Yurok/Getty Images Pro

They’re kind of like super glue. They work great and keep just about anything together for a long time if you take care of them. But if you leave the cap off? The magic glue dries up quickly and the entire bottle dies, with no way to revive it. Only the trash lies in its future.

It’s similar with telomeres and telomerase. At the tip of our chromosomes are telomeres, little “caps” that keep cells functioning well. The longer the telomere “caps,” the healthier the cells. Telomerase? Closely related, this enzyme is associated with keeping telomeres long and healthy. If telomerase decreases, and telomeres on cells shorten with age (basically fraying), this is associated with cellular degradation and age-related diseases, including cancer.

So what’s mindfulness got to do with it? Genetics play a role in aging, as we know, and lifestyle, too. Everything from what we eat, whether we exercise, stress and sleep levels, anxiety, depression, and smoking, all of it can impact telomere length and telomerase. Focusing on activities that increase telomere length and telomerase are gradually being shown to support health, too, contributing to positive aging and longevity.

No big corporations are running out to spend money on researching how meditation or yoga might lengthen your telomeres or extend your life, so evidence is accumulating slowly, but it’s accumulating nonetheless.

Here are several things we’ve learned, with surely more to follow:

  • Regular yoga practice or meditation have both been associated with longer telomeres and increased telomerase. You can choose to do one without the other, if you like. Yoga and/or meditation are associated with decreased stress and anxiety, improved mood, calmer nervous system activity, and physical strength and agility. These mindful activities benefit mood regulation, attention, and cognitive well-being as well.
  • It makes sense yoga and meditation—time-honored mindfulness practices over millennia—contribute to health. Their ability to improve mood, stress, and well-being have a self-reinforcing effect. We feel better after we meditate or practice yoga, so we’re more likely to rinse and repeat, even if sporadically.
  • It makes little difference what form of yoga or meditation you practice, only that you do it consistently enough for benefits to accrue. Yes, more time meditating or practicing yoga seems to have more salutary effects on telomeres and telomerase (and thus to decrease cellular aging), but you can start and tap into the “feel-good” effects of brief mindfulness meditations or yoga any time, even for a few minutes. Just start where you are.
article continues after advertisement

It doesn’t matter if you’re 9 or 90. Beginning or increasing a yoga or meditation practice at any age offers benefits. You needn’t hole yourself up in a mountain cave spending hours a day meditating or expect yourself to practice yoga six times a week. In fact, for beginners, just a few minutes is better than more—novices are more likely to stick with it in shorter bursts, and sticking with it is what matters. It’s about the long game, and telomeres and telomerase play the long game, too. A little meditation or yoga feels good, so start low and go slow. And be compassionate with yourself in the process—self compassion has been found to lengthen telomeres, too.

item.title: Why Optimists Live Longer
item.description:
Optimism

Why Optimists Live Longer

How a hopeful mind lowers inflammation, even when life is hard.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • Optimism is linked to living four to eight years longer and a lower risk of premature death.
  • Optimism benefits the body by reducing inflammation and strengthening stress resilience.
  • Optimism is a trainable skill, not a fixed personality trait.
  • Three simple habits—gratitude, future visualization, and using your strengths—can boost optimism.
Source: David Baileys/iStockphoto

Optimism and Longevity

Optimism has long been dismissed as little more than positive thinking, but growing evidence suggests it is a powerful biological asset. Large prospective cohort studies and meta-analyses show that people with higher levels of optimism live 5–15 percent longer, have a 13–14 percent lower risk of death from any cause—even after accounting for depression, health behaviors, and chronic illness—and, on average, live four to eight years longer than their less optimistic peers; however, the exact benefit varies across populations. 1

The evidence extends beyond lifespan. A meta-analysis combining data from more than 220,000 people found that optimists were about one-third less likely to develop cardiovascular disease and 14 percent less likely to die during the study period than less optimistic individuals. 2 Remarkably, the protective effect of optimism was comparable to that of many traditional cardiovascular risk factors. A second meta-analysis involving more than 180,000 people reached the same conclusion: people with a more optimistic outlook consistently had a lower risk of premature death. 3

How can something as intangible as optimism affect the body?

Scientists believe it works through several interconnected pathways. First, optimists and their partners’ optimism are associated with better cognitive functioning.4 Second, optimists are more likely to engage in healthy behaviors, including regular exercise, nutritious eating, restorative sleep, and avoiding smoking.5 Third, people with a more optimistic outlook tend to have lower levels of chronic inflammation, healthier cholesterol profiles, and a better-balanced autonomic nervous system, which helps the body recover more efficiently from stress. 5,6,7 Fourth, optimists are more likely to cope adaptively with setbacks, cultivate supportive relationships, and remain resilient during adversity.

The evidence is compelling enough that the American Heart Association recognizes optimism as a psychological factor linked to better cardiovascular health and greater longevity. Importantly, optimism is not fixed—it can be strengthened through targeted interventions that may benefit both mental and physical health.

Some research suggests that reducing pessimism may be just as important as increasing optimism because pessimism itself appears to harm health.9

How to become more optimistic:

If you are having a less-than-inspired life right now, being optimistic may seem out of reach. However, there are several ways to boost your optimism.

article continues after advertisement

Intervention 1: Optimism doesn't mean pretending your life is perfect or ignoring hardship. It simply means believing that your future can be better than your present.10 At its core, optimism is your brain's ability to generate a positive prediction about what lies ahead.11 One way to strengthen that prediction is to remind yourself that change is possible. Ask yourself: Has anyone who has faced challenges like mine eventually turned their life around? The answer is almost always yes. That gives your brain real-world evidence that difficult circumstances don't have to be permanent. Instead of predicting more of the same, your brain can begin to imagine a different future with the best possible self.12

Intervention 2: Before you go to bed, write down three good things that happened during the day and, just as importantly, why they happened.13 They don't have to be life-changing. Perhaps someone smiled at you, you completed a task you'd been avoiding, or you enjoyed a great cup of coffee. The key is to train your brain to notice what is going right rather than automatically focusing on what is wrong.

This simple exercise has surprisingly powerful effects. In a study involving more than 10,000 people across 34 countries, practicing gratitude increased optimism, positive emotions, and life satisfaction.14 Other research has shown that the benefits could last for at least six months.

Why does it work? Gratitude gives your brain evidence that good things are happening. Instead of scanning the world for threats or disappointments, your brain begins to recognize patterns of positive experiences.15 Over time, this shifts its predictions.

Intervention 3: Take a few minutes to identify four of your greatest character strengths—such as curiosity, kindness, perseverance, creativity, or gratitude.16 Then, over the next week, intentionally use each of those strengths in a new way every day. 17 For example, if kindness is one of your strengths, do something unexpectedly thoughtful for someone else. If curiosity is a strength, learn something new or ask deeper questions in a conversation.

Research suggests that regularly using your signature strengths increases happiness, reduces depressive symptoms, and enhances overall psychological well-being. More intensive strengths-based programs have also been shown to increase optimism, suggesting that consistently applying your strengths helps your brain develop a more positive outlook on the future. 18

article continues after advertisement

Conclusion: The message from the science is clear: optimism is not simply a way of seeing the world—it is a way of shaping your future. By training your brain to expect positive possibilities without denying reality, you may not only feel better today but also improve your chances of living a longer, healthier life.

item.title: What Your Emotions Are Actually For
item.description:
Emotions

What Your Emotions Are Actually For

Each emotion has a purpose—even the ones you would rather not feel.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • Many people raised with emotional neglect learn to see their feelings as weak, sappy, or useless.
  • In truth, every emotion has a purpose, even uncomfortable ones like fear, anger, and sadness.
  • Emotions are a built-in survival system, and they fuel the connections that make life meaningful.
Source: New Africa/Adobe Stock

"Although many of us may think of ourselves as thinking creatures that feel, biologically we are feeling creatures that think." –Dr. Jill Bolte Taylor, neuroscientist and author of My Stroke of Insight.

Stupid, sappy, mushy, melodramatic, insipid, tiresome, wimpy, lame. These are all words that I have heard people use to describe their own emotions.

As a psychologist, I see in our society a poor tolerance for something that’s a deeply personal, biological part of who we are as humans: our emotions. Indeed, if you grew up in one of the many, many households where emotion was discouraged or poorly tolerated (childhood emotional neglect), you may now, as an adult, have a negative connotation to feelings of all kinds. You may see emotions as a sign of weakness.

You may hide your feelings from yourself and others, even the people you care about the most. You may regard the expression or sharing of feelings as maudlin, illogical, or just plain useless. You may have no idea what you feel or why, because you have buried your emotions so deeply, even from yourself.

This is childhood emotional neglect, and it is not about anything your parents did to you. Instead, it’s about what didn’t happen for you, the acceptance of your feelings that you needed and did not get. Most emotionally neglectful parents are doing their best, and many were raised in the very same way. It is so often no one's fault. But when you grow up this way, you learn to treat your own emotions as a problem to manage away, rather than the gift they actually are.

Why We Have Emotions at All

Why did emotion evolve in the first place? Sometimes, especially to emotionally neglected people, emotions feel like a burden. Wouldn't it be better if we didn't have to feel sad when we had a conflict with a friend, angry when someone cuts us off in traffic, or anxious before a job interview? On the surface, maybe it would seem easier if we didn't have to feel those things. But I believe that if we didn't have emotions, life would not be better. In fact, it would not be sustainable.

Emotion is necessary for survival. Emotions tell us when we are in danger. They tell us when to run, when to fight, and what is worth fighting for. Emotions are our body's way of communicating with us and driving us to do things. Here are some examples of the purposes of just a few emotions.

9 Emotions and Their Specific Functions

article continues after advertisement
  • Fear tells us to escape for self-preservation.
  • Anger pushes us to fight back, for self-protection.
  • Love drives us to care for spouses, children, and others.
  • Passion drives us to procreate, create, and invent.
  • Hurt pushes us to correct a situation.
  • Sadness tells us we are losing something important.
  • Compassion pushes us to help others.
  • Disgust tells us to avoid something.
  • Curiosity drives us to explore and learn.

You get the idea. For every emotion, there is a purpose. Emotions are incredibly useful tools to help us adapt, survive, and thrive.

Notice that some of these are feelings you would rather not have. Fear, anger, hurt, sadness. They are uncomfortable for a reason. But uncomfortable is not the same as useless. Often, the feelings you most want to push away carry the most important messages of all, because they are the ones warning you, protecting you, or telling you that something matters to you.

People who were emotionally neglected in childhood were trained to try to erase, deny, push underground, and in some cases, be ashamed of this invaluable built-in feedback system. Because they are not listening to their emotions, they may be operating at a disadvantage compared to the rest of us. Pushing away this vital source of information can make you vulnerable and potentially less productive. It also makes it harder to experience life to its fullest.

More Than Survival

Emotions do more, though, than drive us to do things. They also feed the human connections that give life the depth and richness that make it worthwhile. It is this depth and richness that I believe provides the best answer to the question, "What is the meaning of life?" Emotional connections to others help us stave off feelings of emptiness as well as existential angst.

article continues after advertisement

This is why so many emotionally neglected people, who have spent years cut off from their own feelings, describe a quiet sense of emptiness even when their lives look full from the outside. The richness is missing because the feelings that create it have been walled off. The good news is that those feelings are not gone. They are waiting on the other side of the wall.

You and Your Feelings

If you have spent a lifetime trying to deny your natural, biological emotional responses, you may at times feel disconnected, empty, or unfulfilled in life. The people who love you may find you distant, self-contained, or aloof. You may find yourself irritable or angry more often than you would like.

Where to Begin

If any of this rings a bell, please know that your emotions are not gone. They have simply been pushed underground, and they can be welcomed back.

Start small. Several times a day, pause and ask yourself, "What am I feeling right now?" You may draw a blank at first. Ask anyway. When a feeling does come, try to put one word to it, and let it tell you what it is there for. If it feels like too much to do on your own, a therapist who understands emotional neglect can help you find your way back to your feelings.

Over time, as you listen to your emotions instead of pushing them away, your emotions can become what they were always meant to be. Not something sappy or weak, but a source of information, energy, and connection that helps you live your life to the fullest.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com.

© Jonice Webb, Ph.D.

item.title: It’s OK to Fall Down; Just Get Up
item.description:
Resilience

It’s OK to Fall Down; Just Get Up

Resilience, redemption, and resurrection in the social media era.

Posted July 13, 2026

Key points
  • Fall down seven times, get up eight.
  • Resilience, redemption, and resurrection are a source of social salvation.
  • Striving for dignity and grace in the face of external criticism is a gift.

There is an oft-quoted aphorism in the samurai tradition, which, loosely translated, intones “Fall down seven times, get up eight.” The Hagakure, from which the axiom is taken, is an often-misinterpreted treatise on Bushido (the warrior’s way) as a code of death. In fact, it is a discourse drawn from conversations between Yamamoto Tsunetomo and Nabeshima Mitsushige, between 1709 and 1716, on the warrior’s path of both living, and dying, well.

Like Miyamoto Musashi’s Sho Rin No Go (Book of Five Rings) and Sun Tsu’s Art of War, the Hagakure, although lesser known outside martial arts circles, has become a staple for those seeking counsel on self-reliance, resilience, effective leadership, and success. At no point in modern times have these ancient tools been more important. Our social media-informed culture, where a single misstep, misunderstanding, casual comment, or simple presence, can bring about ad hominem attacks and abject ruin, demands it.

On Resilience

In terms of social interaction, one of the most important things to recognize is, in the vast majority of situations, it’s not about you. It’s about the other person, and the elements of their own ego they are imposing upon you. Your boss doesn’t marginalize you, or give you menial tasks because they feel you can’t do the job—it’s because they feel threatened. Your supervisor doesn’t criticize you because you’re doing something wrong; it’s because, in their heart of hearts, they know you do the job better than they do. Your partner doesn’t talk down to you because they want to demean you—it’s because they are unsure of you, and—more to the point—unsure of themselves.

Recognizing these dynamics—and emphasizing empathy, rather than our own ego—is key to a kind of social salvation. It is a mercy and a grace we visit upon those who would do us harm, in word, deed, and action, that allows us to stand and move forward, after we’ve been knocked down, whether figuratively or literally. Resilience often relies more on patience—patience for others, patience for us, and patience for the circumstances we confront—than on being strong, whatever that means, and toughing it out. It also relies on accepting and allowing—a trait touted by Buddhist teaching, that can teach us a great deal about how to be in the world with grace and dignity.

On Redemption

Redemption—to redeem—sounds like we’re getting something back from outside ourselves. In this context, what we are reclaiming is, in fact, simply ourselves. Over the past several decades, it has become easier and easier to lose sight of who we are, and our place in the world. Reclaiming ourselves requires us to reset our personal perspective by releasing our attachment to the people, places, and things outside of ourselves, and recognizing we are, quite literally, the captain of our own ship. Our decisions, choices, and actions steer the course. When we fall into the trap of believing others are driving the boat, we lose sight of the shore, and ourselves.

article continues after advertisement

This perspective, and hopefully, this reset, speaks directly to the notion of accepting and allowing. A hyper-aggravating phrase that has seeped into the collective conscience, and, by association, nomenclature, is “It is what it is.” Annoying yes, but also a universal truth. We can’t control the externals; we can only experience them as they are and get a glove in front of that double-hop grounder, before it gets past us.

Redemption, then, is not about get back at those we perceive as having wronged or slightest us, as has, to some extent, become the rule of the day. It is about releasing that petty, and often pointless, perspective to reclaim ourselves, for us. We take back what was stolen from us, by our own misadventure.

On Resurrection

When we think of resurrection, Christian or not, we typically think of the Risen Christ. It’s not nearly that complicated, or amorphous. Resurrection simply means renewal. Like the Phoenix, we rise from the ashes and restore ourselves to an even greater glory—a version of ourselves that has suffered the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune—whether they be self-created, other-imposed, or simply happenstance—and we have stood against that storm to rise, and rise again. This is the essence of dignity, grace, and, most importantly, transformation.

And, there it is—we are the crucible. Whether our social distortion—interior or exterior—is visited upon us by fate, misfortune, or simple chance, we get to remake it—and ourselves—into something, not only helpful, but useful, and, ofttimes, better. Like Johnny Tremain, we find not only renewed purpose, but build a legacy far surpassing those damned slings and arrows. We can, by choice, be reborn into a larger life, painting upon a larger canvas.
